title: Cricket Australia Opens Big Bash League to Private Investment Starting With Melbourne Renegades
excerpt: The governing body will invite bids for the Renegades franchise from the 2027-28 season, opening the door for IPL owners and other investors despite opposition from New South Wales and Queensland.
body:
• Cricket Australia announced private investment will be introduced into the BBL from the 2027-28 season, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.
  • States can sell up to 49% stakes in their franchises under a self-determination model, with IPL franchise owners among potential buyers.
  • New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to privatisation, while Victoria, Tasmania and Western Australia back the plan.
  • CA had originally hoped to raise up to A$600 million (US$432 million) from privatisation to address the sport's financial pressures.

Cricket Australia has approved the sale of Big Bash League franchises to private investors, announcing on Tuesday that the Melbourne Renegades will be the first club taken to market ahead of the 2027-28 season, according to Reuters.

The decision marks the most significant structural change to Australian domestic cricket in decades, opening the door for private capital — including from Indian Premier League franchise groups — to flow into the country's premier T20 competition.

How the Deal Works

Under the approved framework, states will be given permission to sell up to 49% stakes in their BBL franchises to private investors. The Renegades, owned by Cricket Victoria and champions in the 2018-19 season, will go first.

"CA will invite bids from private owners for the Renegades with a view to them playing the 2027-28 season under new ownership," the governing body said. "Pending the result of that process, CA will consider taking other clubs to market under a self-determination model that gives each state member the ability to assess the optimal pathway for its own club and community."

"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash Leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game."

— Mike Baird, Cricket Australia Chairman

A Divided Sport

The announcement follows months of contentious negotiations among state cricket bodies. An earlier proposal in April was scuppered when the boards of New South Wales and Queensland refused to back a unified privatisation plan.

Cricket NSW, which operates the Sydney Sixers and Sydney Thunder, has been the most vocal opponent. According to Fox Sports, NSW chairman John Knox has argued the plan amounts to a quick cash injection that will not solve the sport's long-term financial challenges. Queensland Cricket has raised concerns that privatisation could drive player payments to unsustainable levels while undermining investment in grassroots cricket.

Victoria and Tasmania have ardently supported the sell-off, with Western Australia also on board. South Australia came around after CA scrapped a controversial "holdout tax" that would have penalised states delaying their decision to sell, according to SEN's Tom Morris.

The IPL Factor

The prospect of IPL franchise groups buying into BBL clubs has been a central feature of the debate. IPL owners already control or hold stakes in T20 teams across England's Hundred (MI London, Sunrisers Leeds, Manchester Super Giants), South Africa's SA20, the UAE's ILT20 and Caribbean leagues. The BBL represents one of the last major T20 competitions without Indian franchise ownership.

CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said he believed fears about Indian dominance were overblown. "India are such a huge part of cricket, but we're not looking to sell the game to India. That's it, full stop," he told SEN radio in May. "We are looking to add value to our clubs and bring good partners in, and the decision on who those partners are is at the behest of the states."

Despite a revenue boost from hosting India for a five-Test series, CA reported a net deficit of A$11.3 million for the 2024-25 financial year, underscoring the financial pressures driving privatisation.

BBL Goes to India

In a sign of the growing India-Australia cricket relationship, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced in July that December's BBL season opener between the Renegades and Perth Scorchers will take place in the Indian city of Chennai.

What's Next

The Australian Cricketers' Association is negotiating what share of any sale proceeds players would receive, having previously pushed back on the privatisation timeline. CA plans to involve top-level men's and women's cricketers in the formal announcement. If the Renegades sale proceeds smoothly, other willing states are expected to follow, potentially reshaping the league's ownership landscape by the end of the decade.
